---
title: "1.13 — General completeness of first-order natural deduction"
---

```lean
import Principia.FirstOrder
open Principia.FirstOrder
```

## 1. The question: where do the objects of our countermodel come from?

We now have a consistent theory deciding every formula and supplying existential witnesses.
Our domain will be **all finite terms**, including arbitrarily nested function applications.
The syntax leaf `variable i` can itself serve as a parameter object of this model.

For example, a term model can contain c, f(c), f(f(c)), and every further finite application.
We make no assumption that a small finite domain will suffice.

## 2. Define the interpretation from the theory

`Henkin.model Γ` interprets a function symbol by constructing its term tree:

```text
function f [t₁,...,tₖ] = Term.function f [t₁,...,tₖ]
predicate p [t₁,...,tₖ] holds exactly when
  Henkin.Theory Γ (Formula.predicate p [t₁,...,tₖ]).
```

The identity environment sends index i to the parameter object `Term.variable i`.
`Henkin.term_identity` proves that evaluating any term there returns that term itself.
The predicate interpretation is a Lean proposition about derivability, not an executable
Boolean test. This is a mathematical model, not the search program.

## 3. The truth lemma connects interpretation and membership

The central theorem says, for consistent Γ:

```text
Henkin.truth_lemma hΓ a :
  a.evaluate (Henkin.model Γ) Term.variable ↔ Henkin.Theory Γ a
```

For a predicate, this is how the model was defined. For a conjunction, the theory contains
the pair exactly when it contains both components, by introduction and projection rules.
For a disjunction, completeness of the theory rules out the case where both alternatives
are absent: their negations would refute the disjunction.

Quantifiers are the essential new step. A universal formula in the theory supplies every
term instance by universal elimination. Conversely, if the universal were absent, its negation
would be present. Classical reasoning derives an existential counterexample, and the witness
property supplies a term where the body fails. That contradicts all term instances holding.
An existential is handled directly by its witness and existential introduction.

Instantiation changes terms without changing the body's number of logical connectives.
The Lean proof recurses on that logical size, so it can apply the induction hypothesis to
instances containing larger term trees. Structural induction on the full term/formula size
would not justify that particular recursive call.

## 4. Turn an unprovable conclusion into a countermodel

Suppose Γ does not derive a. Then ¬a :: Γ is consistent: a derivation of falsum from that
context would give a by the classical contradiction rule.

Build the Henkin model for this enlarged context. The truth lemma makes every original
assumption true and makes ¬a true. Thus a is false in this model. We have constructed a
countermodel to the proposed entailment Γ ⊨ a.

Contrapositively, entailment implies existence of a derivation:

```text
deduction_complete : Formula.Entails Γ a → Nonempty (Derivation Γ a)
deduction_iff_entails Γ a :
  Nonempty (Derivation Γ a) ↔ Formula.Entails Γ a
```

The second theorem combines general completeness with the earlier soundness theorem.
It covers arbitrary formulas and finite assumption contexts in our equality-free first-order
language, over arbitrary nonempty domains. The added structural weakening and fresh-index
quantifier variants are explicit constructors with their own checked soundness cases.

## 5. Using completeness is different from running search

Here we use a semantic argument to establish the existence of a proof of a new disjunction:

```lean
example (a : Formula) (valid : Formula.Valid a) :
    Nonempty (Derivation [] (.disjunction a a)) := by
  apply deduction_complete
  intro D inhabited M ρ assumptions
  exact Or.inl (valid D inhabited M ρ assumptions)
```

After `apply deduction_complete`, the goal is entailment. The introductions select an arbitrary
domain, evidence it is inhabited, a model, an environment, and truth of the empty context.
`valid` supplies truth of a there; `Or.inl` builds the semantic disjunction.

This theorem establishes `Nonempty`: some finite derivation exists. Its Henkin construction
uses classical, noncomputable choices, and does not provide a terminating executable validity
decider. The finite search interfaces from 1.11 still return unknown on failure. A separate
eventual-success theorem for those particular implementations has not been proved.

## 6. Prove it

Work in `Skeleton.lean`. These exercises apply the new ideas to statements different from
the worked examples. Try them before reading the corrections.

```bash
make lab C=01-natural-deduction/13-first-order-completeness
```

Combine the two general directions for a closed conclusion.

```lean
theorem closed_proof_iff_valid (a : Formula) :
    Nonempty (Derivation [] a) ↔ Formula.Valid a := by
  sorry
```

Replace each original assumption by a semantic consequence of a different context.

```lean
theorem provability_transfers (Γ Δ : List Formula) (a : Formula)
    (available : ∀ b ∈ Γ, Formula.Entails Δ b) (proof : Nonempty (Derivation Γ a)) :
    Nonempty (Derivation Δ a) := by
  sorry
```

## 7. Graduated hints

### `closed_proof_iff_valid`

**First hint.** Validity is entailment from the empty context.

**Next hint.** Specialize deduction_iff_entails at [].

### `provability_transfers`

**First hint.** Use general completeness after establishing entailment from Δ.

**Next hint.** Soundness interprets the original derivation; available supplies each interpreted assumption.

## 8. Worked corrections

These exact proofs are also in `Solution.lean`, checked by `make test`.

### `closed_proof_iff_valid`

```lean
theorem closed_proof_iff_valid (a : Formula) :
    Nonempty (Derivation [] a) ↔ Formula.Valid a := deduction_iff_entails [] a
```

Formula.Valid is defined as entailment from []. The general equivalence therefore already has the required type; no extra proof construction is needed.

### `provability_transfers`

```lean
theorem provability_transfers (Γ Δ : List Formula) (a : Formula)
    (available : ∀ b ∈ Γ, Formula.Entails Δ b) (proof : Nonempty (Derivation Γ a)) :
    Nonempty (Derivation Δ a) := by
  apply deduction_complete
  intro D inhabited M ρ hΔ
  exact (deduction_iff_entails Γ a).mp proof D inhabited M ρ
    (fun b hb => available b hb D inhabited M ρ hΔ)
```

Completeness changes the requested existence of a derivation into a semantic goal. At an arbitrary model satisfying Δ, available establishes every assumption of Γ. Soundness of the original derivation then gives a.

## 9. Optional practice

Use `optional/Skeleton.lean`. Pending optional proofs are reported separately and do not
fail completed required work.

Relate failure of validity to absence of any closed derivation.

```lean
theorem not_valid_iff_no_closed_proof (a : Formula) :
    ¬Formula.Valid a ↔ ¬Nonempty (Derivation [] a) := by
  sorry
```

*Hint:* Negate both sides of the closed soundness/completeness equivalence.

Establish existence of a proof that projects a universally quantified conjunction.

```lean
theorem quantified_left_projection (p q : Nat) :
    Nonempty (Derivation [] (.implies
      (.universal (.conjunction (.predicate p [.variable 0]) (.predicate q [.variable 0])))
      (.universal (.predicate p [.variable 0])))) := by
  sorry
```

*Hint:* Use completeness; in an arbitrary model, specialize the universal hypothesis and project the first part.

## 10. Optional corrections

These proofs are in `optional/Solution.lean`, included in the checks and exercise reset.

### `not_valid_iff_no_closed_proof`

```lean
theorem not_valid_iff_no_closed_proof (a : Formula) :
    ¬Formula.Valid a ↔ ¬Nonempty (Derivation [] a) :=
  not_congr (deduction_iff_entails [] a).symm
```

The equivalence has validity on the required side after symmetry. not_congr applies negation to both sides of that equivalence.

### `quantified_left_projection`

```lean
theorem quantified_left_projection (p q : Nat) :
    Nonempty (Derivation [] (.implies
      (.universal (.conjunction (.predicate p [.variable 0]) (.predicate q [.variable 0])))
      (.universal (.predicate p [.variable 0])))) := by
  apply deduction_complete
  intro D inhabited M ρ assumptions h x
  exact (h x).1
```

After applying completeness, the target is semantic entailment. The quantified hypothesis can be applied to an arbitrary object x, yielding a pair. Its first component proves the interpreted predicate at x.

## 11. Conclusion

Every semantic consequence of a finite context has a finite natural-deduction derivation, and every derivation is semantically sound. Henkin extensions and the truth lemma establish the missing general direction. This mathematical existence theorem is distinct from completeness or termination of a particular proof-search implementation.
